plants.common_name: Philodendron 'Royal Queen' (tag; taller, roots on top)
plants.container: Clear nursery pot inside a grey fluted pot, bark and perlite mix, white hand-written stake
plants.id_basis: A white hand-written stake reads 'Philodendron Royal Queen'. It is a self-heading philodendron with thick red-pink leaf stalks. A true 'Royal Queen' (a Philodendron erubescens hybrid) has very dark, burgundy-black leaves; these are orange, peach and yellow-green. Ethan says it has been in direct sun for a while, which can bleach dark philodendron leaves toward bronze and yellow, so the tag may be right. The colours fit 'Prince of Orange' just as well.
plants.id_alternatives:
Philodendron 'Royal Queen' (as tagged, sun-faded)
Philodendron 'Prince of Orange'
Philodendron 'McColley's Finale'
Philodendron 'Black Cardinal' (also bronze when young)
plants.id_improve:
The colour of the next new leaf after a few weeks in bright shade (indoors, or the covered porch)
Where it was bought, and the store tag or receipt
plants.temp_notes: Leaf margins scorch or tan with chilling near 50 F. Frost kills.
plants.humidity_notes: The tan crispy edges could come from dry air.
plants.light_notes: The tan edges and yellow bleached patches suggest sunburn, cold nights or dry air. Give filtered light.
plants.winter_summary: Tropical foliage plant. Bring it inside before nights fall under 55 F.
plants.winter_triggers: Target Nov 1; before any night under 50 F.
plants.winter_steps:
Target: indoors by about Nov 1, before the first night forecast under 50 F.
Pre-move: rinse the leaves with a hose, check undersides and stem nodes for spider mites, mealybugs, scale and fungus gnats, treat with insecticidal soap or neem, then quarantine 2 weeks away from other houseplants.
Acclimate in two steps to limit leaf drop: about a week on the covered porch or in the garage, then inside.
Do not repot or fertilize for the move; trim only dead tissue.
plants.indoor_setup:
Indoors: within 3 ft of an east or south window, or under a full-spectrum grow light 12-14 h/day at 6-12 in. Winter sun in Round Rock is only ~4.5-6 hours of real sunshine per day in Dec-Jan, so supplement.
Indoor winter air is typically 20-35% RH; raise it with a humidifier (target 50-60%), grouping plants, or a pebble tray, and keep plants away from heater vents.
Water when the top 2 in dry; reduce in winter.
Check leaf undersides for thrips and spider mites.
plants.health_summary: Growing, with several crowns and new leaves, but the leaves are sun-faded to orange and yellow-green, the lower stem is bare with dry papery leaf bases, and roots are showing on top of the mix.
plants.health_observations:
Leaves orange, peach and yellow-green (likely sun-faded)
Thick red-pink leaf stalks
Two or more crowns
Dry, papery old leaf sheaths at the base (normal)
Roots exposed on top of the mix
One leaf with a small hole
Two small rounded seedlings (weeds) at the base
plants.health_steps:
Cover the exposed roots with an inch of fresh mix, or repot a little deeper.
Move it out of direct sun into bright shade (indoors, or the covered porch). Sun bleaches the leaves and scorches them.
Bring it in before nights fall below 55°F.
Water when the top inch of mix is dry; feed at half strength in spring and summer.
Pull the small seedlings at the base.
plants.notes: Photographed on November 1, 2026, on the porch bench. Ethan: no page until now.
plants.water_notes: Water when the top 1-2 in (3-5 cm) of mix is dry. Soak until water drains out, then empty the saucer. Indoors in winter this stretches to every 10-14 days. Cold, wet mix is the commonest way to lose these plants.
plants.soil_medium: Chunky, fast-draining aroid mix: about 40% potting soil, 30% orchid bark, 20% perlite or pumice and 10% coco coir or worm castings. The pot must have drainage holes.
plants.fertilizer: Balanced liquid, such as 3-1-2 or 20-20-20, at half strength
plants.nutrients: Feed every 2-4 weeks from March to September at half strength, and stop from November to February. Pale new leaves point to low nitrogen. Yellow older leaves with green veins point to low magnesium (1 tsp Epsom salt per gallon, once a season). Brown crisp tips can be salt build-up: flush the pot with plain water every 2-3 months.
plants.pests_watch:
Spider mites: fine webbing and stippled leaves, worst in dry heated air
Thrips: silvery streaks and black specks on leaves
Mealybugs: white cottony clumps in leaf joints
Fungus gnats: small flies over damp mix
Root rot from cold, soggy mix
Bacterial or fungal leaf spot: brown, water-soaked spots
plants.pest_steps:
Check leaf undersides and leaf joints once a week, and before any plant comes indoors.
Keep newly moved plants apart from the others for 2 weeks.
Wipe leaves with a damp cloth to remove dust and mites.
For mites, thrips or mealybugs: spray insecticidal soap or neem oil every 5-7 days for three rounds. Test one leaf first and do not spray in hot sun.
For mealybugs on a few spots: touch each with a swab of 70% rubbing alcohol.
For fungus gnats: let the top inch of mix dry, add yellow sticky traps, and water once with Bti (Mosquito Bits) soaked water.
Remove leaves with leaf spot, keep the foliage dry and give the plant airflow.
plants.growth_habit: Evergreen tropical aroid, a self-heading or slowly climbing hybrid
plants.height_ground: Not grown in the ground here; 2 to 4 ft where it is
plants.zone_notes: Damaged below about 50°F; a houseplant here.
plants.native_range: A cultivated hybrid or mutation, with no wild range. Its parents are Philodendron species from tropical Central and South America.
plants.danger_humans: All parts contain needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing them causes burning pain and swelling of the mouth, tongue and throat, drooling and trouble swallowing; the sap can irritate skin and eyes. Rarely serious, but keep it from children and wash your hands after pruning.
plants.danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): the calcium oxalate crystals cause pawing at the mouth, drooling, mouth swelling, vomiting and trouble swallowing.
plants.propagation:
Stem or node cuttings rooted in water, moss or moist chunky mix.
Separate offshoots (pups) with their own roots from the base.
Many of these hybrids can revert or change pattern when grown from cuttings; tissue-cultured plants keep the look best.

plants.location: Porch bench, on a terracotta saucer
plants.container: Black nursery pot on a square terracotta saucer, with its yellow barcode tag
plants.id_basis: The yellow barcode tag reads 'Alocasia Frydek', and the leaves fit it: arrow-shaped, velvety (Ethan felt them), with a pale midrib and pale main veins. Frydek leaves are usually deep green; these are lighter, which fits a young plant in bright light. It is a third Alocasia, separate from P-056 and P-061.
plants.id_alternatives:
Alocasia micholitziana 'Frydek'
Alocasia 'Green Velvet' (a trade name for the same plant)
Alocasia 'Maharani' (thicker, grey leaves; less likely)
plants.id_improve: A daylight photo of a full-grown leaf
plants.temp_notes: Collapses below about 55 F; the tuber survives above about 38 F if kept barely damp. Frost kills it.
plants.humidity_notes: Dry indoor air invites spider mites.
plants.light_notes: Direct afternoon sun scorches the leaves.
plants.winter_summary: Tropical and cold-sensitive. Bring it in before nights fall under 55 F.
plants.winter_triggers: Target Oct 28; before any night under 55 F.
plants.winter_steps:
Target: indoors by about Oct 28, before the first night forecast under 55 F.
Pre-move: rinse the leaves with a hose, check undersides and stem nodes for spider mites, mealybugs, scale and fungus gnats, treat with insecticidal soap or neem, then quarantine 2 weeks away from other houseplants.
Acclimate in two steps to limit leaf drop: about a week on the covered porch or in the garage, then inside.
Do not repot or fertilize for the move; trim only dead tissue.
Expect leaf loss; keep the mix barely damp and be patient in spring.
plants.indoor_setup:
Indoors: within 3 ft of an east or south window, or under a full-spectrum grow light 12-14 h/day at 6-12 in. Winter sun in Round Rock is only ~4.5-6 hours of real sunshine per day in Dec-Jan, so supplement.
Indoor winter air is typically 20-35% RH; raise it with a humidifier (target 50-60%), grouping plants, or a pebble tray, and keep plants away from heater vents.
Keep the mix lightly moist and above 60 F.
Check leaf undersides weekly for mites.
plants.health_summary: Putting out several new leaves, but they are lighter than a Frydek should be, one has a dry pale patch at the tip, and spotted spurge is spreading over the pot.
plants.health_observations:
Velvety arrow-shaped leaves with pale midribs
Several new leaves and shoots
Leaves paler green than usual for Frydek
One leaf with a dry, pale patch at its tip
Spotted spurge (a weed with thin red stems and small maroon-spotted leaves) is growing in the pot.
plants.health_steps:
Pull the spotted spurge with gloves on, roots and all, before it sets more seed. Its milky sap irritates skin and is toxic to pets.
Give it bright shade, not direct sun: Frydek leaves bleach and scorch in sun.
Keep the mix lightly moist, never soggy; Alocasias rot in cold wet soil.
Bring it in before nights fall below 60°F; it may drop leaves in winter and regrow from the corm in spring.
Wipe the leaves now and then and check the undersides for spider mites, which love Alocasias.
plants.notes: Photographed on November 1, 2026. Ethan: the third Alocasia, and the 'fuzzy pale-green-leaved plant' on the photo list.
plants.water_notes: Keep the mix lightly moist but never soggy: water when the top inch is dry. Cold, wet mix rots the tubers, so cut water back as nights fall below 60 F. If the leaves die back in winter, keep the mix barely damp and wait for spring.
plants.soil_medium: Chunky aroid mix with extra perlite: about 40% potting soil, 30% perlite or pumice, 20% orchid bark and 10% coir. Drainage holes are essential.
plants.nutrients: Feed every 2 weeks at half strength while it is growing (April to September). Stop in cool weather. Yellowing lower leaves are normal as it grows; many yellow leaves at once usually mean overwatering.
plants.pests_watch:
Spider mites (the most common problem; stippling and fine webs under leaves)
Thrips and aphids on new leaves
Mealybugs near the base
Tuber and root rot in cold, wet mix
Fungus gnats
plants.pest_steps:
Check leaf undersides and leaf joints once a week, and before any plant comes indoors.
Keep newly moved plants apart from the others for 2 weeks.
Wipe leaves with a damp cloth to remove dust and mites.
For mites, thrips or mealybugs: spray insecticidal soap or neem oil every 5-7 days for three rounds. Test one leaf first and do not spray in hot sun.
For mealybugs on a few spots: touch each with a swab of 70% rubbing alcohol.
For fungus gnats: let the top inch of mix dry, add yellow sticky traps, and water once with Bti (Mosquito Bits) soaked water.
Remove leaves with leaf spot, keep the foliage dry and give the plant airflow.
plants.growth_habit: Tropical perennial from a rhizome or corm (an aroid); can go dormant in cool or dry spells
plants.growth_rate: Fast in summer, slow or dormant in winter
plants.lifespan: Many years; the corm survives dormancy
plants.zone_notes: Leaves are damaged below about 50°F. A dormant plant loses its leaves but can regrow from the corm in spring if kept just moist.
plants.native_range: The genus grows wild from tropical Asia to eastern Australia. Houseplant kinds like these are mostly cultivated hybrids.
plants.bloom: A cream spathe, occasional on mature plants.
plants.fruit: Red berries after flowering. Not edible.
plants.danger_humans: All parts contain needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing them causes burning pain and swelling of the mouth, tongue and throat, drooling and trouble swallowing; the sap can irritate skin and eyes. Rarely serious, but keep it from children and wash your hands after pruning.
plants.danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): the calcium oxalate crystals cause pawing at the mouth, drooling, mouth swelling, vomiting and trouble swallowing.
plants.propagation:
Separate offset corms ("bulbils") found in the soil when repotting, and start them in damp moss or perlite.
Divide clumps in spring.

plants.aliases: Store tag: 'Monstera' (water once a week; medium to bright indirect light; 65-85°F)
plants.location: Porch bench (shelf with the yellow edge)
plants.container: Maroon nursery pot inside a grey pot, peat and perlite mix, printed 'Monstera' tag
plants.id_basis: The printed store tag reads 'Monstera'. Many slim green stalks come up close together, each with one glossy, heart-shaped, unsplit leaf, and each stalk has a winged sheath at its base: the way young Monstera deliciosa grown from seed looks before its leaves start to split. Stores often plant several seedlings in one pot.
plants.id_alternatives:
Monstera deliciosa (young, seed-grown)
Monstera borsigiana (the smaller, faster form of deliciosa)
Rhaphidophora tetrasperma (less likely: its young leaves are narrower)
plants.id_improve: A photo of the next leaf: splits or holes would confirm deliciosa

plants.health_summary: Healthy and full: many young plants with glossy green leaves. Several old stalks have been cut or broken off near the base, and the pot is crowded.
plants.health_observations:
Many young stalks in one pot, each with a heart-shaped unsplit leaf
Glossy, firm leaves; a few pale from bright light

plants.health_steps:
Give it bright light but not hours of direct afternoon sun, which pales and scorches the leaves.
Bring it in before nights fall below 55°F.
Water when the top inch is dry; let the outer pot drain so it never stands in water.
In spring, split it into two or three pots, or move it to a bigger pot with a moss pole: crowded seedlings stay small.
Pull off the dry sheaths and stubs once they come away easily.

plants.zone_notes: Damaged below about 50°F; a houseplant here. Grown outdoors in South Florida and Hawaii.

plants.conservation_status: No IUCN Red List assessment that Claude could confirm.
plants.invasive: Not a risk in Central Texas.

Indoors: within 3 ft of an east or south window, or under a full-spectrum grow light 12-14 h/day at 6-12 in. Winter sun in Round Rock is only ~4.5-6 hours of real sunshine per day in Dec-Jan, so supplement.
Indoor winter air is typically 20-35% RH; raise it with a humidifier (target 50-60%), grouping plants, or a pebble tray, and keep plants away from heater vents.
Water when the top 2 in of the mix are dry; reduce watering in winter.
Keep the pole damp to encourage aerial roots to grab it.
plants.health_summary: Alive and putting out new split leaves from the base, but the main stems have been cut back and lost most of their leaves, and the oldest stem section is dry and papery.
plants.health_observations:
A cluster of new, split leaves low on the plant
Main stems cut back to bare green canes with aerial roots
Oldest stem section brown, dry and papery

plants.health_steps:
Leave the bare green canes: each node can sprout a new leaf. Remove only stem sections that are brown and hollow.
Tie the new growth up the stake as it lengthens; it climbs and gets bigger leaves when it can grip something (a moss pole is best).
Bright light, but not hours of direct afternoon sun.
Bring it in before nights fall below 50°F (the tag says keep above 50°F).
Water when the top inch is dry, about weekly in summer and less in winter.
plants.notes: Ethan's photos of November 1, 2026: the 'climbing aroid beside the Monstera' on the photo list.
plants.water_notes: Water when the top 1-2 in (3-5 cm) of mix is dry. Soak until water drains out, then empty the saucer. Indoors in winter this stretches to every 10-14 days. Cold, wet mix is the commonest way to lose these plants.
plants.soil_medium: Chunky, fast-draining aroid mix: about 40% potting soil, 30% orchid bark, 20% perlite or pumice and 10% coco coir or worm castings. The pot must have drainage holes.
plants.fertilizer: Balanced liquid, such as 3-1-2 or 20-20-20, at half strength
plants.nutrients: Feed every 2-4 weeks from March to September at half strength, and stop from November to February. Pale new leaves point to low nitrogen. Yellow older leaves with green veins point to low magnesium (1 tsp Epsom salt per gallon, once a season). Brown crisp tips can be salt build-up: flush the pot with plain water every 2-3 months.
plants.pests_watch:
Spider mites: fine webbing and stippled leaves, worst in dry heated air
Thrips: silvery streaks and black specks on leaves
Mealybugs: white cottony clumps in leaf joints
Fungus gnats: small flies over damp mix
Root rot from cold, soggy mix
Bacterial or fungal leaf spot: brown, water-soaked spots
plants.pest_steps:
Check leaf undersides and leaf joints once a week, and before any plant comes indoors.
Keep newly moved plants apart from the others for 2 weeks.
Wipe leaves with a damp cloth to remove dust and mites.
For mites, thrips or mealybugs: spray insecticidal soap or neem oil every 5-7 days for three rounds. Test one leaf first and do not spray in hot sun.
For mealybugs on a few spots: touch each with a swab of 70% rubbing alcohol.
For fungus gnats: let the top inch of mix dry, add yellow sticky traps, and water once with Bti (Mosquito Bits) soaked water.
Remove leaves with leaf spot, keep the foliage dry and give the plant airflow.
plants.growth_habit: Evergreen climbing tropical vine (an aroid) with aerial roots
plants.zone_notes: Damaged below about 50°F; a houseplant here. Grown outdoors in South Florida and Hawaii.
plants.native_range: Southern Mexico to Panama, in tropical forest.
plants.conservation_status: No IUCN Red List assessment that Claude could confirm.
plants.invasive: Not a risk in Central Texas.
plants.bloom: A cream spathe around a thick spadix, on mature plants; rare indoors.
plants.fruit: Mature plants grow a long green fruit, the "fruit salad" fruit. Fully ripe flesh is edible, tasting of pineapple and banana; unripe fruit is full of irritating crystals. Rarely forms indoors.
plants.danger_humans: All parts contain needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing them causes burning pain and swelling of the mouth, tongue and throat, drooling and trouble swallowing; the sap can irritate skin and eyes. Rarely serious, but keep it from children and wash your hands after pruning. Only fully ripe fruit is safe to eat.
plants.danger_animals: Toxic to cats and dogs (ASPCA): the calcium oxalate crystals cause pawing at the mouth, drooling, mouth swelling, vomiting and trouble swallowing.
plants.propagation:
Stem cuttings with a node and an aerial root, in water, moss or moist chunky mix.
Air layering on a tall plant.
Seed, rarely available.

data.summary: A fast climbing aroid with split leaves, sold as 'Mini Monstera'; grown for looks.

uses.text: Climbs a pole or trellis indoors; the leaves split more as it climbs.
uses.caution: Contains calcium oxalate crystals: chewing it burns the mouth. Keep it away from pets and children.

compost.why: Soft leaves and stems rot quickly; wear gloves when chopping it.

partners_good.name: Monstera
partners_good.why: Same light, water and humidity; both climb a moss pole.

partners_bad.name: Cacti and other succulents
partners_bad.why: They need full sun and dry soil, which this plant does not.

propagation.how: Cut below a node with an aerial root and root it in water or moss; new leaves come in 3 to 6 weeks.
Pin a node onto moist mix in a second pot; cut it free once it has rooted.

breeding.text: It rarely flowers indoors, so crossing it at home is not practical.
